newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin to seek higher EU growth if French left wins.
newsitem.headline: Jospin to seek higher EU growth if French left wins.

text.p: Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on Wednesday he would seek British support at a European Union summit next month to boost EU economic growth if the left wins France's parliamentary election.

Jospin said the Socialists aimed to bolster growth by stimulating consumption and fostering higher pay if the left wins an upset victory over the ruling centre-right in the May 25-June 1 vote. But he ruled out any dramatic wage hikes.

"I want France to lead with its European partners a policy of stronger growth," Jospin told RTL radio, saying he saw no reason why Europe should lag behind the United States, Japan, or south-east Asia.
If elected, he said one of the Socialists' first initiatives would be to push for higher EU growth at next month's EU summit in Amsterdam.

Jospin said he would base the drive "notably on the change that has just taken place in Britain", referring to Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair's victory on May 1 that ended 18 years of Conservative rule.

The Socialist leader reiterated that France would not fully meet budget deficit criteria for qualifying for a single European currency from 1999. "I think personally...that the respect for Maastricht will not be met to the nearest centime," he said.

He said he believed the Socialists' criteria for taking France into a single currency -- including entry of Italy and Spain from the start -- were "realistic and that we have a good chance of obtaining them".

Jospin said French voters were more in tune with the Socialist views on Europe than those of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, which he said laid too much stress on austerity needed to qualify for the euro.

Opinion polls show that 85 percent of French people favour reviving consumption by hiking salaries -- a key demand of the Communist party with which Jospin would almost inevitably have to share power in an uneasy coalition.

"The share of salaries in national wealth is too small...we have to reestablish a better balance between what goes to capital and what goes to salaries and so to consumption. That needs to be done progressively," he said.
But he refused immediate hikes. "I don't want a quick blaze that burns out, a surge of salaries which then forces us into austerity," he said.
France's Socialists campaign platform comprises cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay and creation of 700,000 youth jobs.

The latest poll, a CSA survey, projected that the ruling coalition would win 317 seats out of 555 in mainland France, the Socialists and their allies 215, Communists 22 and the far-right National Front one.
